lessons.sub: A big center and easy development

lessons.title: The London setup
lessons.sub: Bishop out first, then e-pawn, knight, c-pawn, knight, bishop
lessons.why: Half of club players answer the d-pawn with theirs. This order of moves meets almost all of them.
lessons.outcome: A solid position where you choose the plan

lessons.title: Black offers the dark bishops
lessons.sub: Step back; if Black takes, the h-pawn takes back
lessons.why: One club player in four puts the bishop opposite yours as soon as the e-pawn moves. Keep yours, and the trade costs Black a semi-open h-file.
lessons.outcome: Your rook already looks at the h-pawn

lessons.title: The queen goes for the b-pawn
lessons.sub: Queen out in front of the b-pawn: offer the trade
lessons.why: The one real try against the setup: your dark bishop has left the queenside and the b-pawn has no guard.
lessons.outcome: Equal, and Black has spent time on the queen

lessons.title: The Steinitz Countergambit: the knight trick
lessons.sub: C-pawn at home? Knight out, and the pawn grab loses
lessons.why: When Black's c-pawn goes two squares before your c-pawn has moved, the queen raid on the b-pawn walks into a knight. Six in ten club players take the pawn.

lessons.title: Knight first, then the bishop at your knight
lessons.sub: C-pawn, then the queen hits the b-pawn
lessons.why: A third of club players bring the queen's knight out on move two. When the light bishop then comes at your knight, it leaves the b-pawn behind.
lessons.outcome: Black has to give up the b-pawn or bend the queenside

lessons.title: Knight and bishop at the c-pawn
lessons.sub: Offer the bishops; the queen check wins the knight
lessons.why: With the knight out, Black's bishop and knight can both aim at your c-pawn. Trading the bishop takes that away, and one club player in eight jumps the knight at your queen anyway.

lessons.title: Black's bishop comes out first
lessons.sub: Light bishop out at once; the queen takes back
lessons.why: One club player in eight copies your idea and brings the light bishop out on move two. It is Black's best minor piece: offer yours for it.

lessons.title: The c-pawn guards the d-pawn
lessons.sub: Same setup; offer the bishops, take if it stays
lessons.why: A small share of club players, but it is your own Black setup from the other side. The bishop rule is the same as everywhere.
lessons.outcome: Black's pawns are doubled; you are slightly better

lessons.title: The King's Indian setup
lessons.sub: Bishop one square, h-pawn one square, castle
lessons.why: The most common answer to your bishop after the knight: three club players in ten put their bishop behind the g-pawn.
lessons.outcome: Comfortable, and the e-pawn push costs Black a pawn

lessons.title: The e-pawn: back to the setup
lessons.sub: The same moves reach the same position
lessons.why: Two club players in ten answer your bishop with the e-pawn. Most of the time the d-pawn follows and you are in the setup lesson.

lessons.title: The small d-pawn
lessons.sub: The e-pawn push loses a pawn
lessons.why: One in seven. Black wants the e-pawn push; with your bishop on the diagonal, it just drops a pawn.
lessons.outcome: A pawn up, or the fianchetto lesson

lessons.title: The d-pawn two squares
lessons.sub: Back to the London by another road
lessons.why: Two in ten. Every position here is one you already know from the first chapter.

lessons.title: The c-pawn hits the d-pawn
lessons.sub: Push past, knight out, then the e-pawn
lessons.why: Rare, but sharp. Pushing past gains space and keeps Black's c-pawn out of the game.

lessons.title: The Horwitz Defense
lessons.sub: The same setup by another road
lessons.why: One club player in nine starts with the e-pawn. It nearly always ends in the setup.

lessons.title: The Englund Gambit
lessons.sub: Take the pawn; when the queen grabs, the knight comes out
lessons.why: One in thirty-five, and the players who choose it are hoping for the trap. Know the one move that avoids it and you are a clean pawn up.
lessons.outcome: A pawn up and a safer king

lessons.title: The Old Benoni
lessons.sub: Push past it, then knight and e-pawn
lessons.why: One in thirty-five. Bringing the bishop out first would walk into the queen raid on the b-pawn; the push past takes the space instead.

lessons.title: The Modern Defense
lessons.sub: The King's Indian setup by another road
lessons.why: One in fourteen between them. They meet the fianchetto lesson, apart from one e-pawn push to know.
lessons.outcome: The fianchetto lesson, or a pawn up

lessons.title: Rare first moves
lessons.sub: The same setup and the same bishop rule
lessons.why: About one game in fifteen between them. None needs anything new.

lessons.title: The setup: fianchetto, then the e-pawn
lessons.sub: Bishop to the long diagonal, e-pawn two squares, knight tucked in, castle
lessons.why: Four in ten club players answer with the e-pawn, and both knights usually follow. The whole setup comes out here, in its usual order.
lessons.outcome: A slow game on your terms

lessons.title: Black opens the middle
lessons.sub: Take the d-pawn; then the king's knight comes out the usual way
lessons.why: One in five pushes the d-pawn at once. Take it, and your bishop's diagonal is wide open.

lessons.title: The bishop comes at your knight
lessons.sub: Carry on; if it takes, the b-pawn takes back
lessons.why: One in five brings the bishop out to trade it for your knight. Let it: you get the two bishops and another pawn for the middle.

lessons.title: The bishop aims at f2
lessons.sub: Bishop out, then the small e-pawn move if the knight jumps
lessons.why: One in five aims the bishop at f2. Your setup doesn't change; one knight jump needs a careful answer.

lessons.title: Other third moves
lessons.sub: The c-pawn gets ready for the d-pawn: go at the e-pawn first
lessons.why: One in twelve plays the c-pawn one square here, to push the d-pawn next. Your king's knight goes at the e-pawn before that happens.

lessons.title: Queen's knight first
lessons.sub: The same setup, by another road
lessons.why: One in seven brings the other knight out first. Nothing changes for you.

lessons.title: The early bishop and the queen
lessons.sub: G-pawn, then the small e-pawn move when the queen comes at f2
lessons.why: One in eight brings the bishop out on move two, often with the queen behind it aiming at f2.

lessons.title: Other second moves
lessons.sub: The bishop at your knight, the small d-pawn, the c-pawn
lessons.why: The bishop on move two, the small d-pawn move, and the c-pawn that gets ready to push the d-pawn.

lessons.title: The Symmetrical
lessons.sub: The same setup; Black often copies it
lessons.why: One in ten copies your first move. Your setup comes out move for move.
lessons.outcome: Equal, and you know the plan

lessons.title: Knight first
lessons.sub: Against the fianchetto the whole setup; against the e-pawn one square, the king's knight first
lessons.why: One in nine starts with the knight and chooses a setup later. Yours is the same against all of them.

lessons.title: The fianchetto at once
lessons.sub: Bishop against bishop on the long diagonals
lessons.why: Black fianchettoes first. The same eight moves.

lessons.title: The d-pawn at once
lessons.sub: Take it; when the queen takes back, the knight comes out with tempo
lessons.why: One in ten pushes the d-pawn on move one. Take it: the queen that takes back loses time to your knight.

lessons.title: The e-pawn one square
lessons.sub: Knight, then take the d-pawn when it comes
lessons.why: One in eleven gets ready for the d-pawn push. When it comes, take it and put your own d-pawn in the middle.

lessons.title: The c-pawn one square
lessons.sub: Knight, take the d-pawn, king's knight out
lessons.why: The same idea with the c-pawn. Take the d-pawn when it comes; the king's knight comes out in front of the f-pawn.

lessons.title: Rare first moves
lessons.sub: The small d-pawn, the f-pawn, the b-pawn
lessons.why: Everything else. The setup does the work.

lessons.title: Odd third moves
lessons.sub: Center pawns first; when a piece hangs, take it
lessons.why: The fianchetto, the early queen, the knight to the rim. Each leaves something loose, and the same c-pawn and d-pawn plan finds it.

lessons.title: The Gunderam and other odd second moves
lessons.sub: Bishop out or d-pawn two squares, then castle
lessons.why: The queen in front of the bishop, the bishop in front of the d-pawn. Black blocks their own pieces: develop and open the middle.

lessons.title: The Borg, the Barnes and other odd first moves
lessons.sub: Both center pawns, then knights and bishops
lessons.why: Edge pawns and the f-pawn on move one. Take the middle with both pawns; one of these loses at once to the queen.

games.title: The shot on f7 you missed four times
games.summary: Black jumped the knight into the center and later brought the bishop out toward your king. Each time, f7 was guarded only by the king and taking it with the bishop won a pawn and wrecked Black's king. The game was lost much later to a tactic on move 18.

games.title: Three chances to push the e-pawn
games.summary: Black stepped the bishop back, a line in your book. Your d-pawn push was fine (the engine even likes it a touch more), but three times the e-pawn push to kick the knight was the strongest move, and each time it was skipped.

games.title: The line that wasn't in your book
games.summary: Black declined your gambit pawn with the quiet d-pawn move, which wasn't in your book yet. Later you missed taking the knight first, and taking on f7, before the long diagonal decided the game.

games.title: Black ignored f7 and paid for it
games.summary: Black attacked your bishop instead of defending f7. You grabbed the rook and won. The bishop capture on f7 is even cleaner; it's in your book now.

games.title: A Fried Liver that mates in 12
games.summary: The textbook Fried Liver. Black's king ran back home, you took the knight, and the king hunt ended in mate.

games.title: The f7 shot in a different opening
games.summary: Black guarded the center pawn with the d-pawn and a knight, then spent a move on the h-pawn. Taking on f7 with the bishop was winning. The quiet bishop move let Black off, and the game was lost much later.

games.title: Pushing past the knight twice
games.summary: The small pawn move and the big center, exactly right. Then Black's knight sat within reach of your d-pawn and pushing it was the best move, twice in a row. You won anyway, by checkmate.

games.title: A piece up, then one queen move
games.summary: Black left the bishop hanging on move five and you took it. You stayed a piece up for twelve more moves. Then your queen went to a square Black's knight covered.

games.title: The queen check you blocked with the queen
games.summary: Black's queen checked you on move three. Blocking with your queen traded queens and took away your lead in development; Black ground out a long ending.

games.title: Six moves: guard the e-pawn first
games.summary: Black's bishop and knight both hit your e-pawn. You moved your other bishop, lost the pawn, then a second pawn and the rook in the corner. Guard the pawn, or push it past the knight.

puzzles.title: Black pushed the b-pawn

puzzles.title: Black's knight stepped back

puzzles.title: Black just castled
puzzles.t: Push the e-pawn: Black's knight must move and your attack starts.

puzzles.title: Bishop takes f7

puzzles.title: Push past the knight

puzzles.title: Same push, one move later
puzzles.t: Still the best move: the pawn kicks the knight and your center rolls forward.

puzzles.title: Block the check
puzzles.t: Block with the bishop. The queen block trades queens and lets Black off the hook.

puzzles.title: Save the e-pawn
puzzles.t: Push it past the knight, or guard it with the bishop. Anything else and it falls.
